title: POC scoping - benchmark harness integration
summary: Initial POC scoping focused on integrating Finlytics' benchmark harness with Redwood's runtime. Covered success criteria (p95 latency & throughput targets), workload sizing, streaming vs non-streaming tests, harness integration points (scripts, auth, artifact locations), timeline (2-4 week pilot with a one-week benchmark run), and next steps including delivering a benchmark template and scheduling infra access. Action items assigned for pricing, benchmark spreadsheet, and repo access.

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-10-14
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (CTO - Finlytics), Priya Nair (ML Engineer), Liam O'Connor (Infra), Ava Martinez (Product)

Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect): Discussed POC scope to validate performance/latency and cost across streaming and non-streaming paths. Determined success criteria and timeline for a 2-4 week pilot; agreed to integrate Finlytics' benchmark harness with Redwood test endpoint; set action items and next steps.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Samir (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — Samir here from Redwood, Maya our SE is on the call as well.
[00:12] Jordan (CTO): Hey Samir, thanks. Jordan here, Priya and Liam and Ava on our side.
[00:18] Maya (SE): Hi all. Today's goal is to scope the benchmark integration and make sure the harness can run both streaming and non-streaming workloads against our dedicated test endpoints.
[00:30] Priya (ML): Yep that's right, we want to validate p95 latency and throughput for a few representative workloads — condense, chat completions, and a 512-token generation job.
[00:40] Samir: Great. Can you share a quick baseline — what does your current harness measure and how do you run load?
[00:47] Priya: Sure. We have a JMeter-based harness but mostly it's a set of Python scripts that run parallel requests from k6 agents. We measure requests per second, token throughput, p50/p95/p99 latencies, and we capture streaming chunk arrival times.
[01:03] Liam (Infra): We typically run load from our GCP project us-east1, eg VM pools that spawn up to 200 clients. For the pilot we'd like to keep the generator in our infra and funnel to Redwood via public egress — unless we do VPC peering for dedicated.
[01:18] Maya: That works. For initial runs we can give you a hosted sandbox endpoint; for Dedicated/Private we support VPC peering. Note sometimes the product names in our docs get munged, we call the dedicated offering "Redwood Dedicated" — can be called Redwood Dedicatedty on auto-transcripts, ha.
[01:34] Jordan: (laughs) that's fine. Important is we can run identical scripts to what we use in A/B today, and we want to compare against Anthropic/OpenAI baselines.
[01:44] Samir: Understood. Let's talk success criteria — you mentioned p95; what numbers are you targeting and what's acceptable tradeoff on cost?
[01:53] Ava (Product): We're aiming for p95 generation latency under 350 ms for our short completion path (<=128 tokens) and under 800 ms for the 512-token job in non-streaming. For streaming we want stable first-byte latency under 150 ms and steady chunk throughput thereafter. Cost target is roughly parity with current provider within +/-20% for comparable quality.
[02:18] Priya: Also want to ensure KV cache behavior and few-shot context doesn't blow up memory — we will include a long-context test (6k tokens) but that's lower priority for the first run.
[02:29] Maya: Good. For benchmarking we'll ask for two modes: non-streaming full-response (sync) and streaming SSE with chunking approximating your frontend behavior. Our runtime supports both; streaming will show lower tail latency for perceived response time but may increase overall token-level cost due to more frequent network hops — we'll quantify that.
[02:46] Priya: Quick question on measuring: how do you recommend we measure token throughput? We prefer tokens/sec aggregated across workers and also per-connection token rates.
[02:55] Maya: Tokens/sec aggregate is fine. We'll also provide hooks in our test endpoint to emit per-request token counts in the response metadata. If your script can parse response headers/meta, that will help.
[03:06] Jordan: On harness integration — our code repo has a folder called benchmarks/finlytics with several scripts: single_request.py, streaming_test.js, load_profile.yaml. We'll share the link after the call.
[03:17] Priya: Yes, expect to see both a streaming harness (node+SSE) and a non-streaming runner (python/k6). We also have input corpora: short prompts, multi-turn chat, and red-team prompts for safety checks.
[03:30] Samir: Perfect. For the POC we propose the following steps: 1) exchange artifacts and credentials; 2) Redwood provides sandbox endpoints and a benchmark template (spreadsheet) with expected metrics; 3) customer runs initial smoke tests; 4) Redwood runs controlled load tests; 5) we analyze results and tune batching/quant profiles; 6) final report. Timeline estimate is about 2-4 weeks depending on infra access.
[03:57] Liam: If we can do VPC peering it'll speed things up — reduces egress complexity. Can you confirm networking prerequisites?
[04:06] Maya: Yes. For Dedicated we do VPC peering, and we'll send a short runbook with CIDR, allowed ports (TLS 443), and NAT egress guidance. For Hosted sandbox it'll be normal public endpoints with API keys; we recommend whitelisting our IPs for stable runs — we'll provide the list.
[04:22] Priya: For load generation we'll likely sustain bursts up to 1500 RPS for a short profile and 300 RPS sustained for longer runs. Need to confirm how Redwood charges for burst vs sustained throughput.
[04:34] Samir: Pricing discussion we'll follow up in the pricing sheet, but for POC we can grant credits and instrument usage — objective is to get apples-to-apples comparisons. We'll include a cost-per-token estimate based on observed token rates and runtime settings.
[04:48] Jordan: On metrics, aside from latency and throughput we also want error rates, model output quality (we'll run our auto-evals), and resource utilization (GPU occupancy) if possible.
[04:59] Maya: We can surface GPU utilization and concurrency signals in our console; for the pilot we'll export a CSV from the runtime with per-run GPU metrics. Note that sometimes kernel selection skews per-request latency at cold-starts — the harness should include warmup runs.
[05:13] Priya: Good call. We'll include warmup sequences. Also, for streaming tests do you support chunk sizes control? Our frontend expects chunk size ~64 tokens.
[05:22] Maya: We have streaming controls and can throttle chunk sizes; we'll note that in the runbook. Streaming semantics: first-byte latency, then chunk cadence — we'll capture both.
[05:31] Ava: Are there any gotchas with quantized models and quality? We care about hallucination rates on specific prompts.
[05:38] Maya: Quantization can slightly impact quality depending on model and tokenization. We'll run a quality regression check against your eval set. If necessary we'll test a higher-precision variant for correctness-critical paths.
[05:50] Jordan: On timeline — what's realistic? We want an initial benchmark report within two weeks if everything goes smoothly.
[05:57] Samir: Realistically: artifact exchange (48 hours), sandbox + creds (2-3 days), smoke tests (48 hours), full benchmark run (3-5 days), analysis and report (2-3 days). That puts best-case ~10 business days; more typical 2-4 weeks if networking or approvals delay.
[06:15] Liam: Approvals are the usual. We'll aim to get the repo and a security point-of-contact. Who on Redwood owns security questions?
[06:22] Samir: Our security contact is Priyanka Rao — we'll include SOC2 artifacts and our security FAQ in the follow-up. I'll attach the security whitepaper and SOC2 link.
[06:31] Priya (customer): Also need audit logging for inference requests — retention policies matter for compliance.
[06:37] Maya: We capture request-level audit logs and can configure retention. We'll include options and cost implications in the docs.
[06:44] Priya: Good. A couple technical items: 1) our harness expects a multipart streaming SSE connection; 2) we need deterministic percentiles — e.g., p95 measured across test window with warmup excluded.
[06:56] Maya: Both doable. We'll make sure the harness script has flags to exclude warmup and to set concurrency. One thing: when you run streaming tests from many clients you might see head-of-line blocking at the client side if connections are multiplexed — recommend dedicated connections per worker.
[07:11] Jordan: Noted. For comparison we also plan to run the same harness against Anthropic and OpenAI — will you accept results in the benchmark template?
[07:20] Samir: Absolutely, our spreadsheet has columns for baseline providers. We'll want raw data as well for verification.
[07:28] Priya: About model selection — which models will you provision? We want parity with current model family (open-llama-ish) and a higher-quality variant for a quality run.
[07:38] Maya: We'll provision two variants: an open-ish LLM tuned for throughput and a higher-precision variant. We'll label them in the runbook. For Dedicated you can pin a model version.
[07:48] Ava: Any thought on KV cache or long-context runs for later phases?
[07:52] Maya: We'll include a separate long-context job (6k tokens) in the backlog; won't be part of the initial p95 targets but we will run quick sanity checks.
[08:00] Samir: Ok let's summarize — action items and timeline. Samir to send pricing + benchmark template; Maya to provision sandbox creds and runbook; Priya to share harness repo and scripts; Liam to check networking and get SSO/security contact; Finlytics to run smoke tests and then full runs. Follow-up call week of Oct 25.
[08:21] Jordan: That aligns. One nit: please include an example streaming test command in the runbook — we have some idiosyncrasies in our Node client.
[08:30] Maya: Will do. We'll include example curl/node/python snippets.
[08:34] Priya: Also can you share a sample of the runtime response metadata (token counts, model variant id) so our parser knows where to look?
[08:42] Maya: Yes — sample response payload and headers will be included.
[08:45] Ava: Are there any limitations around rate-limiting for the sandbox? We don't want intermittent 429s during a controlled run.
[08:52] Samir: For POC we can raise rate limits for specific test windows; we'll coordinate schedules to avoid platform contention.
[08:59] Liam: Sounds good. One more ops question: can we run the load generator from an on-prem cluster if we do private?
[09:05] Maya: Yes, for Private deployments you can run entirely in your network; for hosted we need public egress unless you do VPC peering. We'll include an ops checklist.
[09:14] Jordan: Alright, last thing — quality comparison. We'll run our automatic evaluation suite and share the results; if Redwood shows regression we'll want to flag immediately.
[09:24] Samir: Understood. We'll set up a regression alert in our Optimize tool for the eval set.
[09:29] Priya: Awesome. Thanks everyone.
[09:33] Samir: Thanks all — we'll send the benchmark template and links in the next 24-48 hrs.
[09:36] Ava: Thanks. Bye.
[09:38] Jordan: Thanks, bye.
